input.question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?
input.ground_truth: I've always tied it to the invention of meiosis. Mitosis divides cells, but meiosis make half-cell kits, that can then combine in rapidly expanding numbers of ways. I see it as several billion years of mitosis and then meiosis gets discovered and boom: Cambrian Explosion.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How/Why did organisms go from single cell division to requiring a separate partner to reproduce?

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine you have a toy block. At first, you can just take that one block and make a copy of it. Now you have two blocks. That’s like a single cell splitting and making two cells by itself.

But then, as time goes on, making more and more copies of the same block isn’t as fun or as good as mixing things up a little. If you only make copies of the same block, they’re all exactly the same, and if something bad happens (like a monster wants to eat all your blue blocks), all your blocks are in trouble.

So, sometimes, two different blocks meet and decide to stick together and make a new kind of block that’s a little bit of both. This is like how two different cells (from two different organisms) come together to make a baby that’s a mix of both parents. This mixing helps make new kinds of blocks (or animals or plants) that can be stronger and better at dealing with problems.

So, organisms started needing a partner because it helped make new kinds that are stronger and can handle more things!
